title: Market data — Overview
summary: Market data spans daily indicators (turnover, trades_count, OHLC) and intraday indicators, plus BEST_MKT quotes for spread and mid. Use SYMBOLS/EXCHANGES for labels.
content: Daily metrics come from ATS.SYMBOL_DAILY_INDICATORS (e.g., turnover, trades_count, average price via CLOSE_PRICE). Intraday metrics (volume, turnover) come from ATS.SYMBOL_INDICATORS. Quote-derived measures (spread=offer−bid; mid=(bid+offer)/2) come from ATS.BEST_MKT. Prefer human labels via ATS.SYMBOLS.SYMBOL and ATS.EXCHANGES.EXCHANGE_NAME.

date_semantics.notes: Use half-open ranges for windows; keep results bounded.

title: Daily indicators — turnover, volume, average price
summary: Use SYMBOL_DAILY_INDICATORS for daily turnover, volume, trades_count and OHLC via CLOSE_PRICE, HIGH_PRICE, LOW_PRICE, OPEN_PRICE.For canonical traded value over arbitrary time windows (e.g. top symbols by traded value last 10 days), prefer SUM(ATS.TRADES.VALUE) on ENTRY_DATETIME; see gl-MKT-metrics-traded-value-v1.
content:
• turnover — SYMBOL_DAILY_INDICATORS.TURNOVER
• trades_count — SYMBOL_DAILY_INDICATORS.TRADES_COUNT
• average/close price — SYMBOL_DAILY_INDICATORS.CLOSE_PRICE
• OHLC — use OPEN_PRICE, HIGH_PRICE, LOW_PRICE, CLOSE_PRICE

Group by TRUNC(STATS_DATE,'DD') for daily; TRUNC(STATS_DATE,'MM') for monthly buckets. Use SYMBOL_ID for joins to SYMBOLS when labels are required.

date_semantics.notes: Default date key for market data is STATS_DATE for daily facts.

title: Intraday indicators — volume and turnover
summary: Use SYMBOL_INDICATORS for intraday volume and turnover; ENTRY_DATETIME is the timestamp for bucketing.
content:
Intraday metrics live in ATS.SYMBOL_INDICATORS.
• volume — SYMBOL_INDICATORS.VOLUME
• turnover — SYMBOL_INDICATORS.TURNOVER

Use TRUNC(ENTRY_DATETIME,'DD') for daily buckets. For rolling windows, use analytic functions over TRUNC(ENTRY_DATETIME,'DD').

date_semantics.notes: Use TRUNC(ENTRY_DATETIME,'DD') for daily aggregation from intraday rows.

title: Traded value — canonical definition
summary: Canonical definition of traded value over a time period. Use ATS.TRADES.VALUE aggregated over ENTRY_DATETIME, joined to ATS.SYMBOLS for symbol labels.
content:
Use ATS.TRADES as the canonical source when the user asks for traded value over a time period.

• traded value / total traded value / value traded — SUM(ATS.TRADES.VALUE)
• time key — ATS.TRADES.ENTRY_DATETIME
• symbol label — join ATS.TRADES.SYMBOL_ID to ATS.SYMBOLS.SYMBOL_ID

Guidance:
• For queries like "top symbols by traded value last N days" or "total traded value per symbol", prefer TRADES.VALUE with a date filter on ENTRY_DATETIME.
• SYMBOL_DAILY_INDICATORS.TURNOVER_VALUE is an end-of-day aggregated metric derived from trades. Use it when the user explicitly asks for *daily indicators* (e.g., daily turnover, daily average price, OHLC per day), or when the question is phrased around "daily" stats.
• When the question does not mention daily indicators or end-of-day stats, treat "traded value" as coming from TRADES.VALUE.

date_semantics.notes: Use ENTRY_DATETIME as the primary time key for traded value. For daily buckets, use TRUNC(ENTRY_DATETIME,'DD').

labels_vs_ids: Use SYMBOLS.SYMBOL for human-readable symbol labels; SYMBOL_ID should be used for joins.

title: Quotes — spread and mid from BEST_MKT
summary: BEST_MKT holds best bid/offer; compute spread and mid from BID_PRICE and OFFER_PRICE.
content:
ATS.BEST_MKT provides quote data.
• spread — OFFER_PRICE − BID_PRICE
• mid — (BID_PRICE + OFFER_PRICE)/2

Use ENTRY_DATETIME as the quote timestamp; TRUNC(ENTRY_DATETIME,'DD') for daily aggregates. Join to SYMBOLS/EXCHANGES for labels.

date_semantics.notes: BEST_MKT is intraday; apply TRUNC for daily buckets or filter directly for intraday slices.

title: Labels — symbols and exchanges
summary: Use SYMBOLS and EXCHANGES tables for human-readable labels; keep IDs in joins, labels in SELECT.
content:
For human-readable outputs, join on:
• ATS.SYMBOLS — SYMBOL_ID → SYMBOL (code), SYMBOL_NAME
• ATS.EXCHANGES — EXCHANGE_ID → EXCHANGE_NAME

In queries, keep IDs in GROUP BY and join labels as non-key columns. This avoids inconsistencies and makes filters easier (IDs are stable; labels can change).

date_semantics.notes: Pure dimension tables; no date semantics.

title: Orders — Overview
summary: Orders capture client instructions: who (client/broker), what (symbol/side/quantity/price), and lifecycle states.
content:
ATS.ORDERS holds the core order records. Important columns:
• ORDER_NO — unique key
• CLIENT_ID / BROKER_ID — who placed the order
• SYMBOL_ID, SIDE, QUANTITY, PRICE
• ENTRY_DATETIME — when the order was entered

Lifecycle states (NEW, PARTIAL, FILLED, CANCELLED, etc.) are tracked via ATS.ORDER_STATES. Flags and classifications live in ATS.FLAGS or related mappings. Orders drive executions (TRADES) and may also be rejected (REJECTED_ORDERS).

**Critical**: Only ORDERS has SIDE column ('B'/'S'). TRADES has no SIDE — use BUYER_BROKER_ID / SELLER_BROKER_ID to determine buy/sell role. Using t.SIDE on TRADES causes ORA-00904.

date_semantics.notes: Use ENTRY_DATETIME for creation-based questions; use ORDER_STATES.STATE_TIME for lifecycle timing questions.

title: Orders — classifications & participants
summary: Orders link clients, brokers, symbols and optional flags. Use FLAGS for classifications and EDS_CLIENTS/SUBSCRIBED_BROKERS for names.
content:
Typical joins:
• ORDERS.CLIENT_ID → EDS_CLIENTS.CLIENT_ID
• ORDERS.BROKER_ID → SUBSCRIBED_BROKERS.BROKER_ID
• ORDERS.FLAG_ID → FLAGS.FLAG_ID

Use these joins when questions mention clients, brokers, or flag descriptions. Keep numeric IDs for grouping; expose labels in SELECT.

date_semantics.notes: Classification does not change the date key; use ENTRY_DATETIME unless explicitly lifecycle-based.

title: Orders — fixed-income fields (yield, accrued profit) & filtering
summary: For fixed-income instruments, orders may carry yield, accrued profit and other bond-specific fields. Use SYMBOL_TYPES to filter bonds.
content:
When orders relate to bonds:
• Use SYMBOL_TYPES to filter fixed-income instruments
• Orders may have YIELD, ACCRUED_PROFIT or similar fields depending on schema

Filter by SYMBOL_TYPES.ASSET_CLASS or similar to isolate bonds; apply yield filters at either order or trade level depending on question.

date_semantics.notes: Same date semantics as generic orders, but limited to bond-like instruments.

title: Trades — Overview
summary: Trades represent executed orders: notional, volume, price, buyer/seller and settlement details.
content:
ATS.TRADES holds executed transactions.
Key fields:
• TRADE_ID — unique trade key
• SYMBOL_ID, QUANTITY, PRICE
• BUY_CLIENT_ID / SELL_CLIENT_ID (or participants via brokers)
• TRADE_DATE, SETTLEMENT_DATE
• NOTIONAL (PRICE * QUANTITY) and possibly YIELD for bonds

Cancel and state information may live in CANCELLED_TRADES and TRADE_STATES. Negotiated trades are linked via NEGOTIATED_TRADES.

**Critical**: TRADES has NO SIDE column. There will be a time when we will have to distinguish between the types of symbols which were traded, For that We will have to go towards the SYMBOL_TYPES table. Where this information will reside and in exact these spellings, i.e SYMBOL_TYPE_ID and SYMBOL_TYPE : 1- EQUITIES,2- Bond,3- ETF . Use SELLER_BROKER_ID for sell-side, BUYER_BROKER_ID for buy-side. t.SIDE → ORA-00904. For sell-side volume/notional, filter on SELLER_BROKER_ID. For buy-side, use BUYER_BROKER_ID. Never join on both unless aggregating total activity.

date_semantics.notes: Pick TRADE_DATE for trading flow questions, SETTLEMENT_DATE for settlement-focused questions.

title: Trades — notional, volume, yield
summary: Use TRADES for notional, traded volume and yield (for fixed-income).
content:
• traded volume — SUM(QUANTITY)
• notional — SUM(PRICE * QUANTITY) or NOTIONAL column if available
• yield — YIELD column when dealing with bonds

Group by TRADE_DATE or SETTLEMENT_DATE depending on the business question.

date_semantics.notes: Prefer TRADE_DATE for market-activity questions; SETTLEMENT_DATE for post-trade/settlement questions.

title: Trades — participants and attribution
summary: Use EDS_CLIENTS and SUBSCRIBED_BROKERS to attribute trades to clients/brokers; buyer/seller sides may both be relevant.
content:
Typical joins for participant attribution:
• BUY_CLIENT_ID / SELL_CLIENT_ID → EDS_CLIENTS.CLIENT_ID
• BUY_BROKER_ID / SELL_BROKER_ID → SUBSCRIBED_BROKERS.BROKER_ID

For questions like “top clients by volume”, aggregate over both buyer and seller roles unless explicitly constrained.

**Side-specific logic**:
• Sell-side activity → use SELLER_BROKER_ID / SELL_CLIENT_ID
• Buy-side activity → use BUYER_BROKER_ID / BUY_CLIENT_ID
• Total activity (e.g. top broker) → UNION ALL or GROUP BY both sides

**Never use t.SIDE on TRADES**. For notional: SUM(PRICE * QUANTITY).

date_semantics.notes: Attribution does not change date semantics; TRADE_DATE remains the primary key unless settlement-focused.

title: Trades — trade vs settlement date
summary: TRADE_DATE is for trading activity; SETTLEMENT_DATE is for cash-flow and settlement questions.
content:
Use:
• TRADE_DATE — when analyzing volumes, market activity, client flow
• SETTLEMENT_DATE — when analyzing settlement cash flows, yields vs settlement, or levies that are settlement-based

Some metrics (like levies) may join trades by TRADE_ID but be keyed on SETTLEMENT_DATE.

date_semantics.notes: Choose date based on the narrative: execution vs settlement.

title: Trades — canonical joins
summary: Trades join to symbols, clients, brokers, settlement types and possibly levies.
content:
Common joins:
• TRADES.SYMBOL_ID → SYMBOLS.SYMBOL_ID
• TRADES.CLIENT_ID / BUY_CLIENT_ID / SELL_CLIENT_ID → EDS_CLIENTS.CLIENT_ID
• TRADES.BROKER_ID / BUY_BROKER_ID / SELL_BROKER_ID → SUBSCRIBED_BROKERS.BROKER_ID
• TRADES.SETTLEMENT_TYPE_ID → SETTLEMENT_TYPES.SETTLEMENT_TYPE_ID

For bond metrics, join SYMBOL_TYPES to filter instrument universes.

date_semantics.notes: Joins do not alter trade date semantics.

title: Rejected Orders — Overview
summary: Rejected orders capture invalid or failed instructions, with reasons stored in REJECTIONS lookup.
content:
ATS.REJECTED_ORDERS stores orders that were rejected before entering the active book.
Key fields:
• REJECT_ID (THIS ONE IS IMPORTANT SINCE IT HELPS IDENTIFY THE CODE, THERE IS NO COLUMN NAMED REJECTION_CODE ) / ORDER_NO
• CLIENT_ID, SYMBOL_ID, MARKET_ID
• REJECTION_ID / REJECTION_ID
• ENTRY_DATETIME or REJECTION_DATETIME

Reasons and descriptions live in ATS.REJECTIONS.

date_semantics.notes: Use rejection timestamp as date key for rejection stats.

title: Rejected Orders — date keys
summary: Use the rejection timestamp for time-series of rejections; original order ENTRY_DATETIME is secondary.
content:
• primary key — REJECTED_ORDERS.REJECTION_DATETIME (or equivalent)
• ENTRY_DATETIME may differ if validation is asynchronous

For daily counts, use TRUNC(REJECTION_DATETIME,'DD').

date_semantics.notes: Rejections are naturally dated by when they were rejected, not when originally submitted.

title: Rejected Orders — typical joins & participants
summary: Rejected orders can be analyzed by client, broker, exchange and symbol; reasons join via REJECTIONS.
content:
Key joins:
• REJECTED_ORDERS.REJECTION_ID → REJECTIONS.REJECTION_ID
• REJECTED_ORDERS.CLIENT_ID → EDS_CLIENTS.CLIENT_ID
• REJECTED_ORDERS.BROKER_ID → SUBSCRIBED_BROKERS.BROKER_ID
• REJECTED_ORDERS.SYMBOL_ID → SYMBOLS.SYMBOL_ID
• REJECTED_ORDERS.MARKET_ID → EXCHANGES.EXCHANGE_ID

date_semantics.notes: Joins add context; time stays keyed on rejection timestamp.

title: REJECTIONS — lookup table, join rule, matching by text
summary: REJECTIONS holds rejection codes and descriptions; join by REJECTION_ID and filter via DESCRIPTION when queries mention textual reasons.
content:
ATS.REJECTIONS typically contains:
• REJECTION_ID
• REJECTION_ID
• DESCRIPTION (e.g., INVALID SYMBOL, INVALID MARKET)

Use DESCRIPTION filters for natural-language questions like “invalid client”, “expiry invalid” etc. Map phrases to LIKE filters on DESCRIPTION.

date_semantics.notes: Lookup table — no time semantics by itself.

title: REJECTIONS — mapping phrases to DESCRIPTION filters
summary: Map natural language reasons (invalid client, invalid market, expiry invalid) to DESCRIPTION filters in REJECTIONS.
content:
Examples:
• “invalid client” → DESCRIPTION LIKE '%INVALID CLIENT%'
• “invalid market” → DESCRIPTION LIKE '%INVALID MARKET%'
• “expiry invalid” → DESCRIPTION LIKE '%EXPIRY INVALID%'

Combine with date and participant filters from REJECTED_ORDERS for richer analysis.

date_semantics.notes: Text-only filters; time semantics come from REJECTED_ORDERS.

title: Cancelled trades — Overview
summary: Cancelled trades represent reversals or voided executions; often analyzed alongside normal trades. Sometimes queries require to check and show the clients information too for which we use the columns like BUYER_CLIENT_ID, SELLER_CLIENT_ID, Similar case for the buyer seller trade id in same case as them, similar for broker as well. Depends upon what is asked.
content:
ATS.CANCELLED_TRADES stores cancelled executions.
Typical uses:
• count of cancellations by date, exchange, symbol
• cancellation ratios vs executed trades (by count or notional)

States may also be tracked in TRADE_STATES.

date_semantics.notes: Use cancellation timestamp for time series of cancellations.

title: Negotiated trades — Overview
summary: Negotiated trades are pre-arranged deals that later execute in the market; they link NEGOTIATED_TRADES to TRADES.
content:
ATS.NEGOTIATED_TRADES contains requests/agreements for negotiated transactions.
Link to ATS.TRADES via a common key (e.g., NEG_TRADE_ID or mapping table).

Typical metric: how many negotiated trades actually execute, and at what notional/price vs intended.

date_semantics.notes: Use request time for pipeline; trade date for executed flows.

title: Levies — Overview
summary: Levies are fees or charges applied to transactions, recorded in LEVIES and related tables; settlement levy data links levies to trades and clients.
content:
Levies can be:
• transaction levies (per trade)
• settlement levies (per settlement event)

Core tables:
• ATS.LEVIES — configuration of levy types
• ATS.LEVY_TYPES — labels and categories
• ATS.SETTLEMENT_LEVY_DATA — actual levy records by trade/client/settlement
• ATS.ATS_LEVY_DATA_LOG or similar — logs by day/market/side

For ATS.SETTLEMENT_LEVY_DATA in particular, the fact table is naturally keyed by TRANSACTION_DATE as the date grain; do not invent alternate levy date grains for this table. When users talk about “levies” or “levy paid” in aggregate (e.g., total levy paid, least levy paid), they are referring to the monetary levy_amount measure on settlement or log tables, not to searching in LEVY_TYPES text.

date_semantics.notes: Pick levy log date for logs; settlement or trade date when levies attach directly to trades. For ATS.SETTLEMENT_LEVY_DATA specifically, treat TRANSACTION_DATE as the canonical date grain and avoid constructing synthetic levy date grains.

title: Levies — amounts and records
summary: Use SETTLEMENT_LEVY_DATA and levy logs to compute total levy_amount and record counts. For settlement levy data, use TRANSACTION_DATE as the sole date grain for time filtering and bucketing.
content:
Core measures:
• levy_amount — amount charged per event/record
• records — COUNT(*) of levy rows

Group by levy type, client, market, or side as needed. Logs may pre-aggregate by day/market/side.

Natural-language phrases such as “levy”, “levies”, “levy paid”, “total levies”, “least levy paid”, “highest levy paid”, etc. map to the monetary measure SUM(LEVY_AMOUNT) on the relevant fact table (e.g., ATS.SETTLEMENT_LEVY_DATA or ATS.ATS_LEVY_DATA_LOG), not to searching for the word “levy” in LEVY_TYPES or filtering by levy type text. Only bring LEVIES/LEVY_TYPES into the query when the user explicitly asks to break levies down by type or configuration (e.g., Trading Charges vs Maintenance Fee).

For ATS.SETTLEMENT_LEVY_DATA, treat TRANSACTION_DATE as the only valid date grain: when questions refer to time windows (e.g., “in 2021”, “last month”, “by day”, “by month”), apply filters and groupings on SETTLEMENT_LEVY_DATA.TRANSACTION_DATE and do not derive alternative levy date keys for this table.

date_semantics.notes: Use levy log date for logs; settlement date when tied to settlements. For settlement levy facts in ATS.SETTLEMENT_LEVY_DATA, always use TRANSACTION_DATE as the time key for filtering and bucketing and avoid creating synthetic levy date grains.

title: Levies — participants and type labels
summary: Join levy data to clients, brokers and levy types for meaningful labels.
content:
Typical joins:
• SETTLEMENT_LEVY_DATA.CLIENT_ID → EDS_CLIENTS.CLIENT_ID
• SETTLEMENT_LEVY_DATA.BROKER_ID → SUBSCRIBED_BROKERS.BROKER_ID
• SETTLEMENT_LEVY_DATA.LEVY_ID → LEVIES.LEVY_ID
• LEVIES.LEVY_TYPE_ID → LEVY_TYPES.LEVY_TYPE_ID

When reporting by levy type, surface user-friendly labels from LEVY_TYPES (e.g., DESCRIPTION) rather than numeric IDs. Example levy types include:
• ID = 1, CODE = 'MAINTENANCE_FEE', DESCRIPTION = 'Member Maintenance Fee'
• ID = 2, CODE = 'TRADING_CHARGES', DESCRIPTION = 'Trading Charges'
• ID = 3, CODE = 'ORDER_CANCELLATION', DESCRIPTION = 'Order Cancellation'

Use these type labels when a question explicitly asks for levies by type (e.g., Trading Charges vs Maintenance Fee); otherwise, when users talk about “levy paid” in general, they usually mean the monetary levy_amount measure, not a specific levy type.

date_semantics.notes: Participant attribution does not change levy date semantics.

title: Levies — date keys and entry timestamp
summary: Use levy log date for logs, settlement date for settlement-linked levies; trade date is secondary. For ATS.SETTLEMENT_LEVY_DATA specifically, use TRANSACTION_DATE as the canonical date grain for all time filters and groupings.
content:
Levy-related dates:
• LEVY_DATE (logs) — when levy was recorded in log
• SETTLEMENT_DATE — for settlement-linked levies in settlement/clearing contexts
• TRADE_DATE — may be used as a secondary filter when linking back to trades
• TRANSACTION_DATE (ATS.SETTLEMENT_LEVY_DATA) — the canonical date key and grain for settlement levy records

For ATS.ATS_LEVY_DATA_LOG, use LEVY_DATE as the primary date when analysing log-based levies (e.g., daily or monthly levy logs by market/side). For settlement-linked levies where the narrative is about settlements, SETTLEMENT_DATE may be relevant on settlement tables.

For ATS.SETTLEMENT_LEVY_DATA specifically, always treat TRANSACTION_DATE as the sole date grain: all filters like "in 2021", "last month", and buckets like "by day", "by month", or "by year" must be applied on SETTLEMENT_LEVY_DATA.TRANSACTION_DATE. Do not derive or invent alternative levy date grains for this fact table.

date_semantics.notes: Align date choice with narrative: logs vs settlements. For ATS.SETTLEMENT_LEVY_DATA in particular, TRANSACTION_DATE is the canonical time key and grain for all filtering and aggregation; avoid constructing synthetic levy date grains on this table.

title: Levies — slabs, criteria, member/securities applicability
summary: LEVY_RANGES, LEVY_CRITERIA and LEVY_INFO describe slabs, criteria and applicability for levies. LEVY_TYPES holds the configured levy types such as Maintenance Fee, Trading Charges and Order Cancellation.
content:
Configuration tables:
• LEVY_RANGES — ranges/slabs, with min/max and value
• LEVY_CRITERIA — basis (e.g., by security, by member, by trade type)
• LEVY_INFO — links levies to member types, security types etc.

Use these tables when questions ask about configuration, not just actual charged levies.

Levy types configured in LEVY_TYPES typically include entries such as:
• ID = 1, CODE = 'MAINTENANCE_FEE', DESCRIPTION = 'Member Maintenance Fee'
• ID = 2, CODE = 'TRADING_CHARGES', DESCRIPTION = 'Trading Charges'
• ID = 3, CODE = 'ORDER_CANCELLATION', DESCRIPTION = 'Order Cancellation'

Use these configuration values when users ask about levy type definitions or comparisons between levy types; do not confuse levy type names with the monetary levy_amount measure on fact tables.

date_semantics.notes: Configuration is usually static or slowly changing; treat as dimension data.

title: Levies — canonical joins
summary: Levy data joins to trades, clients, brokers and configuration tables for full context.
content:
Common joins:
• SETTLEMENT_LEVY_DATA.TRADE_ID → TRADES.TRADE_ID
• SETTLEMENT_LEVY_DATA.CLIENT_ID → EDS_CLIENTS.CLIENT_ID
• SETTLEMENT_LEVY_DATA.BROKER_ID → SUBSCRIBED_BROKERS.BROKER_ID
• SETTLEMENT_LEVY_DATA.LEVY_ID → LEVIES.LEVY_ID → LEVY_TYPES

Use these joins when answering questions about levies by participant, symbol, or type. When joining ATS.SETTLEMENT_LEVY_DATA into a wider query (e.g., together with trades or participants), continue to use SETTLEMENT_LEVY_DATA.TRANSACTION_DATE as the time key and grain for levy-related filtering and aggregation, even if other joined tables expose additional date columns.

date_semantics.notes: Joins complement settlement-based date semantics. For ATS.SETTLEMENT_LEVY_DATA specifically, TRANSACTION_DATE remains the canonical levy date grain in joined queries.

title: Repo — Overview
summary: Repo contracts are collateralized borrowing/lending transactions; contracts, legs and logs describe them.
content:
Core tables:
• REPO_CONTRACTS — master contract, including rate, haircut, maturity, parties
• REPO_CONTRACTS_CANCELLED — cancelled repos
• REPO_LOG — lifecycle events (entered, executed, cancelled)

Metrics include outstanding notional, daily cash flows by leg, average rate and haircut.

date_semantics.notes: ENTRY_DATETIME for flow of new contracts; MATURITY_DATE for maturity profiles. For contracts ACTIVE or OUTSTANDING at a given analysis date D (e.g. 'repos active 500 days ago'), use INITIAL_DATE and TERMINATION_DATE with the filter INITIAL_DATE <= D AND TERMINATION_DATE > D.

title: Repo — legs, types, contract number, maturity
summary: Repo contracts may have legs (cash vs securities), types (Buy/Sell, BuyBack, etc.) and maturity buckets.
content:
Key structural concepts:
• contract number / REPO_CONTRACT_ID — unique identifier
• legs — underlying buy/sell of securities vs cash
• types — Buy/Sell, BuyBack vs classic repo
• maturity buckets — e.g., ≤7 days, 8–30 days, etc.

These often appear in analytical questions (e.g., cash flows by maturity bucket and exchange).

date_semantics.notes: Maturity buckets are derived from MATURITY_DATE relative to contract date or analysis date.

title: Repo — participants and labels
summary: Repo contracts link to clients, brokers, symbols and exchanges; use standard label tables.
content:
Common joins:
• REPO_CONTRACTS.CLIENT_ID / COUNTERPARTY_ID → EDS_CLIENTS
• REPO_CONTRACTS.BROKER_ID → SUBSCRIBED_BROKERS
• REPO_CONTRACTS.SYMBOL_ID → SYMBOLS
• REPO_CONTRACTS.EXCHANGE_ID → EXCHANGES

Use these when questions mention counterparties, exchanges or instruments explicitly.

date_semantics.notes: Participant labels do not change date semantics.

title: Repo legs and the LEG column semantics
summary: LEG refers to repo legs (initial vs repurchase) in repo-domain tables. When users ask about leg-level volume, cash flows, or rates, prefer REPO_CONTRACTS/REPO_LOG instead of generic TRADES.
content:
Repo legs are modelled explicitly via the LEG column in repo-domain tables (ATS.REPO_CONTRACTS, ATS.REPO_CONTRACTS_CANCELLED, ATS.REPO_LOG, and the repo-specific columns in ATS.TRADES/ATS.CANCELLED_TRADES).

Key rules for the assistant:
• When a user mentions 'leg', 'repo leg', 'initial leg', or 'repurchase leg' in the context of volume, notional, cash flows, or rates, interpret this as a **repo** question unless they clearly specify equities or some other product.
• Prefer ATS.REPO_CONTRACTS (and, where appropriate, ATS.REPO_LOG) as the primary fact tables for repo legs, using ENTRY_DATETIME as the flow date key.
• LEG = 1 is the **initial** leg; LEG = 2 is the **repurchase** leg. Legs come in mirrored pairs on the same CONTRACT_NO.
• For client- or broker-level questions about repo legs, use BUYER_CLIENT_ID / SELLER_CLIENT_ID (or *_BROKER_ID) in REPO_CONTRACTS and aggregate over both sides using UNION ALL.
• Avoid using TRADES.LEG for generic equity trade questions; TRADES.LEG is repo-specific and should only be used when the user explicitly frames the question as repo trades in TRADES.

date_semantics.notes: For flows of new repo contracts or legs, use REPO_CONTRACTS.ENTRY_DATETIME (and REPO_LOG.ENTRY_DATETIME when working from the log). For active/outstanding repo positions, combine INITIAL_DATE and TERMINATION_DATE per REPO_CONTRACTS guidance.

title: Repo — canonical joins (log, pairing, cancel)
summary: Repo analysis joins contracts to logs and cancelled contracts to compute ratios and event timelines.
content:
Key joins:
• REPO_LOG.REPO_CONTRACT_ID → REPO_CONTRACTS.REPO_CONTRACT_ID
• REPO_CONTRACTS_CANCELLED.REPO_CONTRACT_ID → REPO_CONTRACTS.REPO_CONTRACT_ID

This allows:
• cancellation ratios (cancelled vs total contracts)
• event timelines (entered, executed, cancelled).

date_semantics.notes: Logs carry their own event timestamps; contracts have entry and maturity dates.

title: Repo — rates, haircuts, outstanding, cancel ratio
summary: Compute average repo_rate, repo_haircut, outstanding contracts and cancel ratios over time.
content:
Common metrics:
• repo_rate — average of RATE column by bucket
• repo_haircut — HAIRCUT column
• contracts — COUNT(*) of REPO_CONTRACTS
• cancel_ratio — cancelled contracts / total contracts
• cash_flow — amount of cash exchanged per day/leg

date_semantics.notes: Use ENTRY_DATETIME for flows of new contracts; compute outstanding by comparing MATURITY_DATE to analysis date.

title: Repo — analysis notes
summary: Be explicit about which leg, side and rate you are aggregating; repos can be asymmetric.
content:
Caution points:
• Know whether you are looking at cash leg or securities leg
• Distinguish opening vs closing legs in BuyBack structures
• Repo rate may be stored at contract or leg level; confirm grain

Clarify in queries whether analysis is contract-level or leg-level.

date_semantics.notes: Conceptual notes only.

title: Instruments & Market Context — Overview
summary: Instrument and market dimensions (SYMBOLS, SYMBOL_TYPES, EXCHANGES) provide context like asset class, sector and exchange.
content:
Core dimension tables:
• SYMBOLS — symbol code, name, listing exchange
• SYMBOL_TYPES — asset class, sector, fixed-income vs equity
• EXCHANGES — exchange names and markets

Use these tables to filter universes (e.g., bonds only, equities only) and to provide readable outputs.

date_semantics.notes: Mostly static dimensions; changes are rare and not typically time-keyed.

title: Canonical joins — labels & market triple
summary: Use a consistent join pattern for SYMBOLS/EXCHANGES to avoid duplicate rows and ambiguous filters.
content:
Standard pattern:
• FACT.SYMBOL_ID → SYMBOLS.SYMBOL_ID
• SYMBOLS.EXCHANGE_ID → EXCHANGES.EXCHANGE_ID

This supports the market triple: (symbol, exchange, instrument type).

Keep joins consistent across Orders, Trades, Market data and Repo when referencing instruments.

date_semantics.notes: Joins are cross-cutting; time semantics live in fact tables.

title: Global — time grains and guardrails
summary: Use consistent time grains (day, month, year) and avoid mixing grains in a single query.
content:
Guidelines:
• Pick a single grain per query: day, month, or year
• Use TRUNC(date_col,'DD'/'MM'/'YYYY') to bucket
• Avoid mixing daily and monthly results in one dataset

Enforce sensible limits (e.g., last 6 months, last 365 days) to keep queries performant.

date_semantics.notes: Abstract guidance applicable across all fact tables.

title: Global — date keys and windowing
summary: Each fact domain has a primary date key; use half-open windows and avoid ambiguous FILTERs on multiple dates.
content:
Primary date keys by domain:
• Market data — STATS_DATE (daily), ENTRY_DATETIME (intraday)
• Orders — ENTRY_DATETIME (or STATE_TIME for lifecycle)
• Trades — TRADE_DATE vs SETTLEMENT_DATE
• Levies — LEVY_DATE or SETTLEMENT_DATE
• Repo — ENTRY_DATETIME or MATURITY_DATE
• Rejections — REJECTION_DATETIME

Use half-open intervals [start, end) and avoid mixing multiple date columns in a single WHERE unless clearly justified.

date_semantics.notes: Central guidance; fact-specific docs provide more detail.

title: Client Buy vs Sell notional and Buy/Sell ratio (TRADES)
summary: Use ATS.TRADES to compute client-level buy and sell notional and Buy/Sell ratios over a period. Normalise buyer and seller roles via UNION ALL instead of joining TRADES to EDS_CLIENTS with an OR condition.
content:
When the user asks for client Buy/Sell notional or Buy to Sell ratio, prefer executed trades over orders.

• Source table — ATS.TRADES is the canonical fact table for executed notional (PRICE * VOLUME) keyed by BUYER_CLIENT_ID and SELLER_CLIENT_ID.
• Roles — A client can appear as buyer or seller. To aggregate cleanly per client, build a role-normalised CTE using UNION ALL:
  – First SELECT: BUYER_CLIENT_ID AS client_id, PRICE*VOLUME AS buy_notional, 0 AS sell_notional.
  – Second SELECT: SELLER_CLIENT_ID AS client_id, 0 AS buy_notional, PRICE*VOLUME AS sell_notional.
• Join pattern — Join the role-normalised CTE back to ATS.EDS_CLIENTS on client_id = CLIENT_ID. Avoid joining TRADES directly to EDS_CLIENTS on (BUYER_CLIENT_ID = CLIENT_ID OR SELLER_CLIENT_ID = CLIENT_ID); the OR condition is slow and can lead to confusing aggregations.
• Date filter — Use TRUNC(ENTRY_DATETIME,'YYYY') or a BETWEEN-style range on ENTRY_DATETIME to limit to the current year, e.g. ENTRY_DATETIME >= TRUNC(SYSDATE,'YYYY') AND ENTRY_DATETIME < ADD_MONTHS(TRUNC(SYSDATE,'YYYY'),1).
• Metrics —
  – buy_notional = SUM(buy_notional)
  – sell_notional = SUM(sell_notional)
  – buy_to_sell_ratio = buy_notional / sell_notional, with a guard for sell_notional = 0 (NULL or filter via HAVING).
• Interpretation — High Buy/Sell ratio indicates a client is net buyer in notional terms over the period; low (<1) indicates they are net seller.

Use this pattern whenever questions mention client Buy/Sell notional, Buy/Sell ratio, or similar executed activity ratios over time.

date_semantics.notes: Filter ENTRY_DATETIME to the relevant calendar period (e.g. current year) using range predicates rather than extracting the year from the column.

section: Year start vs year end moves
title: Symbol year-start vs year-end price difference (SYMBOL_DAILY_INDICATORS)
summary: To answer questions about the difference between year-start and year-end prices per symbol, use ATS.SYMBOL_DAILY_INDICATORS with window functions to pick first and last trading day prices.
content:
When the user asks for price differences between the start and end of a year (e.g. "biggest difference in OHLC on year start and year end in 2022"), treat this as:

• Domain — Market data, daily indicators per symbol.
• Tables — ATS.SYMBOL_DAILY_INDICATORS (daily OHLC fact) joined to ATS.SYMBOLS for the label.
• Date filter — Restrict STATS_DATE to the requested calendar year using a half-open range: STATS_DATE >= DATE 'YYYY-01-01' AND STATS_DATE < DATE 'YYYY+1-01-01'. Avoid extracting the year via EXTRACT(YEAR FROM STATS_DATE) in the WHERE predicate.
• First trading day — For each SYMBOL_ID in the year window, use ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY SYMBOL_ID ORDER BY STATS_DATE ASC) = 1 to identify the first trading day and take OPEN_PRICE from that row.
• Last trading day — For each SYMBOL_ID in the same window, use ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY SYMBOL_ID ORDER BY STATS_DATE DESC) = 1 to identify the last trading day and take CLOSE_PRICE from that row.
• Metric — year_ohlc_diff = ABS(last_day_close - first_day_open).
• Output — Return SYMBOL (joined from ATS.SYMBOLS), first_day_open, last_day_close, and year_ohlc_diff, ordered by year_ohlc_diff DESC.

This pattern is different from the high-low range (MAX(HIGH_PRICE) - MIN(LOW_PRICE)) over the year. Use this year-start vs year-end pattern when the question is explicitly about comparing prices at the beginning and end of a year.

date_semantics.notes: Use STATS_DATE as the primary date key for daily market data and apply half-open calendar-year ranges.

title: Quoted spread — correct relative spread (spread as % of mid)
summary: Always compute average relative spread as AVG(spread / mid), never as (avg_sp / avg_mid). This is the industry-standard and only mathematically correct way.
content:
Critical rules when calculating "spread as a percentage of mid-price" or "relative spread" from ATS.BEST_MKT:

• Wrong & dangerous → (AVG(spread) / AVG(mid)) or AVG(spread)/AVG(mid)
  → mathematically incorrect, distorts results, and hits ORA-01476 when mid = 0

• Correct & required → AVG(100 × spread / mid_price)
  → this is what Bloomberg, traders, risk systems and every market microstructure papers mean by "average relative spread"

Implementation checklist (must all be present):
1. Compute per-quote values first:
   spread      = OFFER_PRICE - BID_PRICE
   mid_price   = (BID_PRICE + OFFER_PRICE) / 2
2. Use NULLIF(mid_price, 0) in the denominator → turns zero mids into NULL → safely ignored by AVG()
3. AVG(100 * spread / NULLIF(mid_price, 0))
4. Filter out bad quotes early:
   AND BID_PRICE > 0
   AND OFFER_PRICE > BID_PRICE
5. Strongly recommended: HAVING COUNT(*) ≥ 50 (or 100) to avoid illiquid symbols with 1–2 crazy quotes dominating rankings
6. Show quote_count in output for transparency

Golden Rule that applies to ALL relative metrics (% of price, % of notional, repo rate spread, etc.):
Average of (num/denom) ≠ (avg num)/(avg denom)
→ Always average the ratio, never the ratio of averages.

Use this pattern for any question containing "spread in percent", "spread as % of mid", "relative spread", "basis points spread", "tightest/widest spreads", etc.

date_semantics.notes: Use calendar-day windows (TRUNC(SYSDATE)-N) for 'last N days' questions. For true trading days, a calendar table would be needed.

title: Circular trading / wash-trade detection (round-trip patterns)
summary: Identify brokers or clients engaged in A→B and B→A trades on the same symbol – classic wash-trade / circular trading surveillance pattern.
content:
Circular trading (also called wash-trading or round-tripping) occurs when two parties repeatedly trade the same instrument back and forth.

Detection pattern (used in fs-072 and surveillance queries):
• Take all trades in a window
• For each (BuyerBroker, SellerBroker, Symbol), check if the reverse direction (SellerBroker → BuyerBroker on same Symbol) also exists
• If both directions exist → flag the pair
• Aggregate per broker (or client) to rank by number of circular relationships

Key implementation points:
• Use EXISTS subquery (or self-join) on reversed roles + same SYMBOL_ID
• Exclude self-trades (BUYER_BROKER_ID != SELLER_BROKER_ID)
• Count unique (counterparty, symbol) pairs to avoid double-counting volume
• Typical windows: last 7d, 30d, 90d, or current month

Business use:
• Market integrity monitoring
• Detecting artificial volume / liquidity inflation
• Revenue-sharing or bonus-gaming schemes between brokers

Never confuse with legitimate two-way flow – circular trading is flagged only when the reverse leg actually occurs.

date_semantics.notes: Use half-open rolling windows (e.g., last 30 days) or fixed calendar periods. ENTRY_DATETIME is the execution timestamp.

title: Order states — canonical source and semantics
summary: Order lifecycle states (Submit, Received, PartialFill, Fill, Cancel, Change, Purge, Reject, etc.) are stored in ATS.ORDERS.STATE → ATS.ORDER_STATES.STATE_CODE. This is the ONLY correct source for lifecycle status. Executions themselves live in ATS.TRADES.
content:
Fundamental rule:
• ALL order lifecycle states (including Submit, Received, Cancel, Change, Purge, etc.) are recorded in ATS.ORDERS.STATE → ATS.ORDER_STATES.STATE_CODE.
• NEVER use REJECTED_ORDERS or text search on REJECTIONS.DESCRIPTION for states other than actual rejections.

Canonical STATE_CODE values (exact spellings as used in this system):
  - 'Submit'       → order submitted by user/front-end
  - 'Received'     → accepted by matching engine, live on book
  - 'PartialFill'  → partially executed; some volume remains
  - 'Fill'         → fully executed; no remaining volume
  - 'Cancel'       → cancelled by user or system
  - 'Change'       → amendment (price/volume change) to a live order
  - 'Purge'        → removed by system (e.g., expired GTD orders, purge job)
  - 'Reject'       → rejected order (see REJECTED_ORDERS for reason codes)

Execution vs trades:
• STATE_CODE 'Fill' / 'PartialFill' expresses lifecycle status, not ticket-level executions.
• The actual executions (tickets, executed prices/volumes) live in ATS.TRADES.
• When the user asks for "executed orders", "orders that traded", "execution time/date", you MUST:
  - use ATS.TRADES as the canonical source of execution timestamps and traded quantities;
  - join ATS.ORDERS.ORDER_NO to ATS.TRADES.BUYER_ORDER_NO or ATS.TRADES.SELLER_ORDER_NO on the same EXCHANGE_ID;
  - optionally filter on STATE_CODE IN ('PartialFill','Fill') if the question explicitly cares about final lifecycle state.

Critical mistakes to avoid:
× Wrong: using STATE_CODE = 'Filled' (this value does not exist; use 'Fill').
× Wrong: treating ORDER_STATES as the only source of execution data and ignoring TRADES.
× Wrong: searching REJECTIONS.DESCRIPTION for lifecycle states like 'Purge', 'Cancel', 'Expired'.

Correct patterns:
• For lifecycle distributions (e.g., cancel vs fill vs purge):
  - join ATS.ORDERS to ATS.ORDER_STATES on STATE_ID and group by STATE_CODE.
• For executed orders (orders that actually traded):
  - join ATS.ORDERS to ATS.TRADES via ORDER_NO (buyer/seller) and use TRADES.ENTRY_DATETIME for execution timestamps.
• For combined lifecycle + execution analyses: use BOTH ORDER_STATES and TRADES, but keep their roles distinct.

date_semantics.notes: Use ORDERS.ENTRY_DATETIME for placement time; ORDERS.STATE_TIME for when the current state was set. Use TRADES.ENTRY_DATETIME for execution time; do not infer executions from STATE_TIME alone.

title: Market vs Exchange — correct breakdown
summary: When user says 'market-wise' or 'per market', use ATS.MARKETS.MARKET_CODE via ORDERS.MARKET_ID — NOT EXCHANGES.EXCHANGE_NAME. In this context, the NAME of the MARKET is in the MARKET_CODE or MARKET_DESC, THere is no such Column as MARKET_NAME
content:
Clear distinction:
• MARKET_ID / ATS.MARKETS.MARKET_CODE → logical trading venue (e.g., 'EQ' = Equity, 'FI' = Fixed Income, 'DERIV' = Derivatives)
• EXCHANGE_ID / ATS.EXCHANGES.EXCHANGE_NAME → physical execution venue (e.g., 'DSE', 'CSE')

When a question says:
- 'market-wise', 'by market', 'equity market vs bond market' → use MARKETS.MARKET_CODE
- 'exchange-wise', 'DSE vs CSE' → use EXCHANGES.EXCHANGE_NAME

99% of business questions that say 'market' mean MARKET_CODE, not exchange.

Join pattern:
ORDERS.MARKET_ID → MARKETS.MARKET_ID → MARKET_CODE

title: Market vs Exchange — NEVER confuse them again
summary: 'Market-wise', 'by market', 'equity market', 'debt market' → ATS.MARKETS.MARKET_CODE. Only use EXCHANGES when user explicitly says 'exchange', 'DSE', 'CSE', or 'exchange-wise'.
content:
Iron-clad rule in this database:

When the user says any of these → use ATS.MARKETS.MARKET_CODE
• market-wise / marketwise
• by market
• per market
• equity market, debt market, ETF market, etc.
• MAINBOARD, DEBT, SME, ETF, etc. appear in results

Only use ATS.EXCHANGES.EXCHANGE_NAME when the user explicitly says:
• exchange-wise
• by exchange
• DSE vs CSE
• Dar es Salaam Stock Exchange, Chittagong, etc.

99.9% of business questions that contain the word "market" mean logical market segment (MARKET_CODE), not the physical execution venue.

Canonical join:
ATS.ORDERS.MARKET_ID → ATS.MARKETS.MARKET_ID → MARKET_CODE

Examples of correct MARKET_CODE values you will see:
- MAINBOARD
- DEBT
- ETF
- SME
- PRE-IPO
- DERIVATIVES

Wrong patterns that must be eradicated:
× JOIN ATS.EXCHANGES e ON o.EXCHANGE_ID = e.EXCHANGE_ID
× SELECT e.EXCHANGE_NAME
when the question said "market"

This rule also applies to TRADES, REPO_CONTRACTS, and any fact table that has both MARKET_ID and EXCHANGE_ID.

date_semantics.notes: Dimension choice is independent of time grain.

title: Order lifecycle  (life cycle )— from submission to resolution (states, times, tracking, fill)
summary: Full journey of an order: submission, validation, states (New/Partial/Filled/Cancel/Purged), execution links, cancellation/expiry. Track via ORDER_NO, times, and STATE_CODE.
content:
In capital markets (e.g., stock exchanges), an order's lifecycle is the end-to-end process from client submission to final outcome (fill, cancel, expiry). Key phases:

1. **Submission/Placement**: Order enters system via broker/client (ENTRY_DATETIME). Includes SIDE ('B'/'S'), VOLUME, PRICE, ORDER_TYPE (market/limit/stop), TIF (day/GTD/IOC), FLAG_ID (e.g., iceberg). Study: Who (CLIENT_ID/BROKER_ID/USER_ID/TRADER_ID), What (SYMBOL_ID/EXCHANGE_ID/MARKET_ID).

2. **Validation/Rejection**: Immediate checks (price limits, margin). If fails → REJECTED_ORDERS (with REJECTION_ID → REJECTIONS.DESCRIPTION like 'INVALID SYMBOL'). Study: Rejection rates, common reasons.

3. **Acceptance/New State**: Valid order → order book, STATE_CODE = 'New'. STATE_TIME marks entry. Other orders can interact (e.g., matching).

4. **Execution/Fills**: Matching engine pairs with counterparts. Partial fill → 'Partial' state, update ACTUAL_VOLUME vs VOLUME. Full fill → 'Filled'. Links to TRADES (ORDER_NO → BUYER_ORDER_NO/SELLER_ORDER_NO). Study: Fill rates, time-to-fill (STATE_TIME - ENTRY_DATETIME), slippage (exec PRICE vs order PRICE).

5. **Amendments**: Changes to live order (price/volume) → new STATE_TIME. Schema implies via STATE changes; no explicit amend log.

6. **Cancellation/Expiry/Purge**: User cancel → 'Cancel'. TIF expiry (e.g., DAY at EOD) → 'Expired'. System cleanup → 'Purged'. Study: Cancel ratios, expiry patterns (compare TIF date).

7. **Settlement/Post-Trade**: Filled orders → settlement (SETTLEMENT_TYPE_ID). For bonds: YIELD, ACCRUED_PROFIT.

Tracking in schema:
• Unique ID: ORDER_NO
• History: Group by ORDER_NO, order by ENTRY_DATETIME/STATE_TIME
• States: STATE_ID → ORDER_STATES.STATE_CODE (e.g., 'New', 'Partial', 'Filled', 'Cancel', 'Purged', 'Expired')
• No full audit trail; infer from times/states. For rejections: separate REJECTED_ORDERS.

Common analyses: Time in states, cancel-to-trade ratios, partial fill patterns. Use for compliance (e.g., high cancels = manipulation).

date_semantics.notes: ENTRY_DATETIME for placement; STATE_TIME for changes/expiries. For expiries, compare TIF date.

title: Repo transaction cycle — from leg 1 (initial) to leg 2 (repurchase)
summary: Full lifecycle of a repo: submission, leg 1 (sale/lend), leg 2 (repurchase/borrow return), with rates, haircuts, settlements. Paired by CONTRACT_NO; track via dates and states.
content:
Repos (repurchase agreements) are short-term collateralized loans: party A sells securities to B (leg 1) and agrees to buy back at higher price (leg 2). Used for liquidity, funding. In markets: classic repo (cash lender perspective) or reverse repo (borrower). Key phases:

1. **Submission/Negotiation**: Contract initiated via REPO_CONTRACTS.ENTRY_DATETIME. Includes parties (BUYER_/SELLER_ CLIENT_ID/BROKER_ID/USER_ID), SYMBOL_ID (collateral), EXCHANGE_ID/MARKET_ID (venue), REPO_TYPE (e.g., 'Classic', 'Buy/Sell Back'). Study: Who initiated (ORIGINATOR), internal refs (INTERNAL_REF_NO).

2. **Leg 1 — Initial Leg (LEG=1)**: Cash-for-security transfer. INITIAL_DATE marks start. Metrics: PRICE * VOLUME (initial notional), SETTLEMENT_AMOUNT (cash paid), DIRTY_PRICE (clean + accrued), ACCRUED_PROFIT (interest to date), YIELD (effective rate), PAR_VALUE (face value), MARKET_VALUE (collateral value). Haircut (REPO_HAIRCUT) reduces collateral value for risk.

3. **Contract Terms**: REPO_RATE (interest rate), TERMINATION_DATE (maturity), SETTLEMENT_TYPE_ID (e.g., T+0/T+1). During term: no explicit 'active' state, but infer from INITIAL_DATE <= analysis_date < TERMINATION_DATE. Modifications: CONTRACT_MODIFY_DATE, PREVIOUS_CONTRACT_NO for rolls/extensions.

4. **Leg 2 — Repurchase Leg (LEG=2)**: Security returned for cash + interest. REPURCHASE_PRICE (higher than initial), REPURCHASE_SETTLEMENT_AMOUNT (principal + profit), REPURCHASE_ACCRUED_PROFIT, REPURCHASE_DIRTY_PRICE. Cycle completes at TERMINATION_DATE.

5. **Execution/States**: TRADE_STATE (e.g., 'Executed', 'Pending'), IS_PROCESSED ('Y'/'N'). Fills link to TRADES via ORDER_NOs. Cancellations in REPO_CONTRACTS_CANCELLED (similar structure).

6. **Post-Cycle/Settlement**: Settlement via SETTLEMENT_AMOUNT/REPURCHASE_SETTLEMENT_AMOUNT. Accrued days (ACCRUED_DAYS) for profit calc. Logs in REPO_LOG for events (e.g., ENTRY_DATETIME per action).

Tracking in schema:
• Pairing: Group by CONTRACT_NO, order by LEG (1 then 2).
• Dates: ENTRY_DATETIME (entry), INITIAL_DATE (leg 1 start), TERMINATION_DATE (leg 2 end).
• No explicit history table; infer cycle from paired legs. For cancellations: separate REPO_CONTRACTS_CANCELLED.
• Joins: SYMBOLS (collateral), EXCHANGES/MARKETS (venue), SUBSCRIBED_BROKERS/EDS_CLIENTS/USERS (parties), SETTLEMENT_TYPES (settlement).

Analyses: Maturity buckets (days to TERMINATION_DATE), avg REPO_RATE/haircut, cash flows (SETTLEMENT_AMOUNT leg 1 vs REPURCHASE_SETTLEMENT_AMOUNT leg 2). Use for risk (outstanding repos), funding costs.

date_semantics.notes: ENTRY_DATETIME for new contracts; INITIAL_DATE/TERMINATION_DATE for active cycles (INITIAL <= D < TERMINATION). Buckets: days to TERMINATION_DATE.

title: Orders — time columns (placement, state changes, execution)
summary: Clarifies which time columns to use for order placement (ENTRY_DATETIME), state changes (STATE_TIME), and executions (TRADES.ENTRY_DATETIME). Also gives the canonical pattern for "executed on the same day it was placed" questions.
content:
Core time columns for orders and executions:

• Placement timestamp — ATS.ORDERS.ENTRY_DATETIME
  - When the user says "when was the order placed?", "orders placed in X", use ENTRY_DATETIME.

• Lifecycle/state timestamp — ATS.ORDERS.STATE_TIME
  - When the user asks "when was the order cancelled?", "when did it get filled?", use STATE_TIME together with STATE_CODE from ORDER_STATES.
  - STATE_TIME marks when the current STATE was set (e.g., Cancel, Fill, PartialFill).

• Execution timestamp — ATS.TRADES.ENTRY_DATETIME
  - Executions (trades) are recorded in ATS.TRADES.
  - Use TRADES.ENTRY_DATETIME as the execution time when the question is about "executed", "traded", "filled" in the sense of actual trades.

Canonical pattern: same-day execution vs placement
• To answer questions like "Show me a list of orders which were executed on the same day on which they were placed":
  - Placement date: TRUNC(ATS.ORDERS.ENTRY_DATETIME, 'DD').
  - Execution date: TRUNC(ATS.TRADES.ENTRY_DATETIME, 'DD').
  - Join ORDERS to TRADES on ORDER_NO (buyer/seller) and EXCHANGE_ID, then compare these truncated dates.
  - Example filter: TRUNC(o.ENTRY_DATETIME, 'DD') = TRUNC(t.ENTRY_DATETIME, 'DD').

Things NOT to do:
× Do NOT invent a STATE_TIME column on ORDER_STATES; STATE_TIME lives on ATS.ORDERS.
× Do NOT guess execution timing purely from STATE_TIME when you actually need trade timestamps; use TRADES.ENTRY_DATETIME.
× Do NOT use non-existing STATE_CODE values (e.g., 'Filled'); valid execution-related codes are 'PartialFill' and 'Fill'.

Summary:
• ENTRY_DATETIME → when order was placed.
• STATE_TIME     → when lifecycle state changed (Cancel, Fill, etc.).
• TRADES.ENTRY_DATETIME → when execution actually happened.
• For "same day placed and executed", always compare truncated ORDER.ENTRY_DATETIME vs TRADE.ENTRY_DATETIME.

date_semantics.notes: ENTRY_DATETIME for placement; STATE_TIME for lifecycle changes; TRADES.ENTRY_DATETIME for executions. For "same-day execution" questions, compare TRUNC(ORDERS.ENTRY_DATETIME) vs TRUNC(TRADES.ENTRY_DATETIME).

title: Short vs Normal (long) trades – identification, volume, and analysis
summary: How to correctly identify short-selling trades using the IS_SHORT flag (not SIDE). Enables short-interest, borrow analysis, and regulatory reporting.
content: In ATS.TRADES, short-selling is flagged via IS_SHORT (VARCHAR2): '1' = genuine short sale (borrow required), '0' = normal trade, NULL = treat as normal. Do NOT use SIDE column – SIDE='S' only means sell-side of any trade (including normal sales of owned shares). Key analyses: short volume ratio, short-interest per symbol, borrow/lend desk activity, regulatory short-position reporting. Always use fixed calendar periods (DATE 'YYYY-01-01') for short-interest calculations. Use COALESCE(...,0) so symbols with only short or only normal trades still appear.

date_semantics.notes: For short-interest reporting use strict calendar year/month boundaries, never rolling windows.

title: Complete annual (or periodic) trading report for a single client – canonical pattern
summary: How to produce a full-year trading activity report for any client: orders, executions, rejected orders, levies, repo legs. Critical for client statements, audits, and relationship management.
content:
When a user asks for a 'complete trading report' / 'full activity' / 'annual statement' for a specific client, always follow this exact pattern:
1. Resolve client name → CLIENT_ID via EDS_CLIENTS (case-sensitive, use = not LIKE unless wildcard).
2. Pull metrics from five sources using the same CLIENT_ID:
   • ORDERS (client places → CLIENT_ID)
   • TRADES (client can be BUYER_CLIENT_ID or SELLER_CLIENT_ID → use IN (..., ...))
   • REJECTED_ORDERS (CLIENT_ID)
   • SETTLEMENT_LEVY_DATA (CLIENT_ID + TRANSACTION_DATE)
   • REPO_CONTRACTS (BUYER_CLIENT_ID or SELLER_CLIENT_ID)
3. Use strict calendar year: >= DATE 'YYYY-01-01' AND < DATE '(YYYY+1)-01-01'
4. Never join TRADES only on BUYER_CLIENT_ID (Qwen mistake) – misses all sell-side activity → zero rows.
5. Output as category / metric / value rows (UNION ALL) for readability.
This pattern works for any year – just change the dates. Also usable for monthly/quarterly reports by adjusting the date filter.

date_semantics.notes: Always use fixed calendar boundaries for client reporting (never rolling windows).

title: Complete annual (or periodic) activity report for a single broker – canonical pattern
summary: Full-year broker report: orders, trades, rejected orders, levies, repo legs. Mirrors client report but uses SUBSCRIBED_BROKERS and BROKER_ID + BUYER_BROKER_ID / SELLER_BROKER_ID.
content: When user asks for 'complete report', 'full activity', 'broker report' + broker name: 1. Resolve name → BROKER_ID via ATS.SUBSCRIBED_BROKERS (never EDS_CLIENTS). 2. ORDERS & REJECTED_ORDERS → join on BROKER_ID. 3. TRADES & REPO_CONTRACTS → join on BUYER_BROKER_ID OR SELLER_BROKER_ID (both sides mandatory). 4. Use same UNION-ALL key/value output as fs-083/fs-084. 5. In WITH clause: ONLY the first CTE (broker_lookup) may have (broker_id) column list; all others must be plain → prevents ORA-32039/32040 forever.

date_semantics.notes: Fixed calendar windows only.

title: Complete annual (or periodic) report for a single symbol – canonical pattern
summary: Full-year symbol report covering daily indicators, intraday, orders, trades, rejected orders and repo activity in one clean row.
content: When user asks for 'complete report', 'full activity', 'symbol report' + symbol code + year: 1. Resolve SYMBOL via ATS.SYMBOLS (case-sensitive). 2. Use year_bounds CTE (DATE 'YYYY-01-01' style) for reusable date window. 3. Aggregate each domain separately (daily indicators, intraday, orders, trades, rejected, repo). 4. LEFT JOIN everything to target_symbol → always returns exactly one row with NVL(...,0). 5. Only first CTE may have column list → prevents ORA-32039/32040. 6. Never expose SYMBOL_ID in final output — only SYMBOL label.

date_semantics.notes: Always use half-open fixed calendar windows via year_bounds CTE.

title: Symbol price growth / change calculation – YTD or fixed year (e.g. doubled in value)
summary: How to compute YTD price growth percentage using first trading day open vs last close. Handles zero/null prices safely with filters and HAVING.
content: To find symbols that 'doubled' (>100% growth) or dropped (> -10%): Use (max close - min open)/min open *100 from SYMBOL_DAILY_INDICATORS. Steps: 1. Fixed year window (>= YYYY-01-01 < (YYYY+1)-01-01). 2. Per-row filters in WHERE (OPEN_PRICE <>0 AND NOT NULL, CLOSE_PRICE <>0 AND NOT NULL). 3. Aggregate checks in HAVING (MIN(OPEN_PRICE) <>0 AND NOT NULL). 4. Use NULLIF(MIN(OPEN_PRICE),0) in formula to avoid div/0. For negative change, WHERE percentage_change < -10 and ORDER ASC. Never use avg prices for growth – always first open vs last close.

date_semantics.notes: Strict calendar year windows only; YTD = TRUNC(SYSDATE,'YYYY') to today.
